title: Intermittent Reinforcement (Trauma Bonding)
description: A pattern where kindness, affection, and cruelty alternate unpredictably, creating an addictive emotional roller coaster that binds the victim to the abuser.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: A pattern where kindness, affection, and cruelty alternate unpredictably, creating an addictive emotional roller coaster that binds the victim to the abuser.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: After a violent outburst, an abuser is suddenly tender, apologetic, and promising change (the “honeymoon phase” of the cycle of abuse).
A boss berates you harshly, then the next day gives you unexpected praise or a small perk, making you feel grateful and loyal.
A friend alternates between warm inclusion and icy exclusion, keeping you off-balance and constantly seeking their approval.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Unpredictable mood swings that seem to have no trigger.
Inconsistent responses: the same behavior gets praise one day and fury the next.
The victim walks on eggshells, hyper-vigilant, trying to “earn” the next warm phase.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “I’m so sorry, I’ll never do it again.” (then does it again)
“You’re the best thing that ever happened to me.” (hours after calling you worthless)
“I don’t know why you stay with me, but I’m so glad you do.”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You feel a rush of relief and even love when the abuse stops, confusing peace with joy.
You minimize the bad because the good feels so intense.
You find yourself craving the “good times” even after serious harm.
You defend the abuser to friends who express concern.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Partial reinforcement schedules create the most persistent behaviors. The unpredictability of reward spikes dopamine far more than consistent reward, creating an addiction-like bond. This is the psychological core of trauma bonding.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Recognize the cycle as a pattern, not as proof that “they’re changing.” Chart the timeline: you’ll see a circle, not a line.
Give weight to the behavior, not the apologies. Measure them by their consistency over months.
Reach out to a third party when you feel the addiction pull; they can see the pattern more clearly.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Believing that the “good moments” are the real person and the abuse is the exception.
Staying because the good moments are so good that they feel worth the pain, ignoring the cumulative harm.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A husband comes home drunk, screams at his wife, and smashes a plate. The next morning, he brings her breakfast in bed, apologizes tearfully, and swears he’ll get help. The wife feels overwhelming love and hope. This cycle repeats monthly for years; her bond to him strengthens, not weakens, because the reconciliation feels like a drug.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: The cruelty isn’t the trap—the kindness between cruelties is. Without the hot bath after the cold, the cold would be unbearable. That warmth is part of the cage.
